newsitem.title: FRANCE: French hint at minority sale for France Telecom.
newsitem.headline: French hint at minority sale for France Telecom.

text.p: The French government, three days before publication of a key audit of public finances, on Friday gave its clearest signal yet it could sell a minority stake in France Telecom.

Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn and junior Industry Minister Christian Pierret said in a letter to a government envoy charged with a wide consultation at the group that the state would keep a majority stake.
The Socialist-led government, which swept to power six weeks ago, had suspended the planned partial privatisation of the telecoms operator by the previous conservative government.

Prime Minister Lionel Jospin made a campaign promise that he would consult the company's 165,000 staff before taking any decision about the group's future. The Communist party, which has three ministers in the 26-strong cabinet, is opposed to privatisations.

Strauss-Kahn and Pierret said in a letter to former Labour Minister Michel Delebarre, appointed on Thursday as special envoy, that "France Telecom will keep its current status and thus a majority state shareholding."

"This public company will fulfil all the public services specified by the law, with strict respect for equality and universal access," according to the letter, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters.

The conservatives had planned to sell about 35 percent of France Telecom in the country's biggest initial public offering. The company was estimated to be worth 160-210 billion francs ($26-$35 billion).
The sale, initially due in May, was postponed by a month after President Jacques Chirac called an early parliamentary election and then suspended.
The mission letter stressed France Telecom's role in "maintaining social cohesion" in the country as well as the need to "improve the quality of social relations within the company."
"However, changes may be necessary to facilitate France Telecom's development in a European and international framework," the letter said.
France Telecom had earlier welcomed the appointment of Delebarre while labour unions said they were ready to engage in a debate over the future of the group.
"We welcome the nomination of Michel Delebarre and France Telecom, chairman Michel Bon in particular, are at his disposal," a company spokesman said.
Delebarre has to report back to the government before September 5. "The new government said it needed time to think things over. This appointment means that things are moving," the spokesman added.

The mission allows Jospin to deliver on his election promise to consult France Telecom staff before taking a decision, and gives him time to test resistance to the sale from the three communist ministers in his cabinet.
Company chairman Bon is in favour of a partial privatisation to help France Telecom face the competition in a liberalised French and European market from 1998.
A listing of France Telecom shares would also permit a share swap with ally Deutsche Telekom, which already has a stock market listing.
Financial analysts said the appointment seemed to indicate the government was edging towards a sale.

"If they want to do it this year, they have to take account of STET , or Telecom Italia as it will be called. STET is coming to the market this autumn," said Richard Jones of Yamaichi. However, the Italian parliament still has to amend laws before the sale can go ahead.

While privatisation revenues cannot be used to reduce the budget deficit to qualify for European monetary union, the money can help finance some operations that would otherwise have weighed on the deficit.
Other state-owned groups such as insurer GAN, bank Credit Lyonnais and railways group SNCF need cash.

France Telecom staff are divided on the issue of a sale. The former government won over a lot of opponents by assuming the pension liabilities of the company's staff and guaranteeing their status as civil servants.
The Force Ouvriere union said it was pleased the government had "reopened the privatisation dossier of France Telecom."
The Communist CGT said it was ready for debate and warned against a "fake consultation" saying it hoped "Man would prevail over the law of money."
CGT, the biggest union at France Telecom, is organising a petition among staff against a privatisation. It has 13,000 signatures so far.
